issues.name: Private nuisance – possession and substantial interference
issues.rule: Private nuisance is a substantial, unreasonable interference with a plaintiff's use and enjoyment of land in his possession or immediate right to possession. Interference is substantial if it would be offensive or seriously annoying to a normal, reasonable person in the community (not a hypersensitive one); defendant's intent/negligence or abnormally dangerous conduct is also required (intentional here since Flowers knows and refuses to stop).
keyFacts: Harry bought and moved into the home across the street
light 'extremely bright, casting a glow far beyond Flowers' property'
light coming in his windows 24 hours a day
Flowers refused to turn off the lights after request
issues.analysis: Harry is in possession and constant, extremely bright light through his windows would seriously bother an ordinary resident, so interference is substantial; Flowers knew of the effect and continues, so the conduct is intentional.

issues.name: Private nuisance – unreasonableness (utility vs. gravity of harm)
issues.rule: Even substantial interference is actionable only if unreasonable: the court balances the gravity of the harm (character of the neighborhood, extent, duration) against the utility of defendant's conduct, including whether defendant could reduce the harm at reasonable cost. Compliance with industry standards is relevant but not dispositive.
keyFacts: greenhouse built twenty years ago in a rural area
suburban area expanded and houses built closer
20 workers; $20 million facility; successful business
industry standards; no way to continue business without the light
Harry's home is much like all others in the area
issues.analysis: Utility is real (jobs, business) but the area is now residential and cheap mitigation (shielding, redirecting, shutters) may exist; for damages Harry likely wins on balance, while total shutdown of lighting is harder to justify.

issues.name: Defense – coming to the nuisance / consent / assumption of risk
issues.rule: Coming to the nuisance is not a complete bar to a nuisance claim but is a factor in reasonableness and in the remedy; a plaintiff who knowingly and voluntarily accepts the condition may be found to have consented or assumed the risk.
keyFacts: Flowers put up signs warning prospective residents
Harry saw the signs but figured the light could not be that bad
Flowers argues Harry knew about the issue when he bought
issues.analysis: Harry's knowledge weighs against him and may reduce damages or the weight of his equities, but it does not bar the claim, especially since he did not appreciate the severity and the residential character had changed around Flowers.

issues.name: Public nuisance
issues.rule: A public nuisance is an unreasonable interference with a right common to the general public; a private individual may sue only if he suffered harm different in kind (not just degree) from that of the public.
keyFacts: light casts a glow far beyond Flowers' property
houses all around in the expanding suburb, all similar to Harry's
issues.analysis: Although the light affects the neighborhood, Harry's harm (loss of enjoyment of his home) is the same kind as his neighbors', so no standing for public nuisance.

issues.name: Trespass
issues.rule: Trespass requires an intentional physical invasion of plaintiff's land by a person or tangible thing; intangible invasions such as light, noise or odor are generally treated as nuisance, not trespass (though some courts allow trespass for particulate matter with substantial damage).
keyFacts: light coming in his windows 24 hours a day
Flowers intentionally operates the lighting system
issues.analysis: Light is intangible and causes no physical damage, so trespass will likely fail; nuisance is the proper theory.

issues.name: Intentional infliction of emotional distress
issues.rule: IIED requires extreme and outrageous conduct, intent or recklessness as to causing severe emotional distress, causation, and severe distress.
keyFacts: Flowers refused to turn off the lights
Harry 'could not tolerate the light'
lights are needed for the plants and meet industry standards
issues.analysis: Operating a lawful business with a legitimate purpose is not outrageous and Flowers did not aim to hurt Harry; the claim fails.

issues.name: Negligence / strict liability
issues.rule: Negligence requires duty, breach, causation and damages; strict liability attaches only to abnormally dangerous activities or animals/products. Bright greenhouse lighting is neither.
keyFacts: Flowers's facility is completely up to industry standards
no physical injury alleged
issues.analysis: Neither theory fits well: compliance with industry standards and absence of physical harm or abnormal danger make nuisance the sole realistic claim.

issues.name: Remedy – injunction
issues.rule: An injunction is an equitable remedy available when legal remedy is inadequate; for nuisance courts balance the hardships/relative equities and public interest, and may deny it or tailor it (limit hours, shielding, redirect lights), sometimes conditioning on plaintiff paying costs where he came to the nuisance.
keyFacts: Harry asked Flowers to turn off the lights
no way to continue the business without the light
Flowers employs 20 workers and invested $20 million
issues.analysis: Total shutoff is unlikely because the hardship to Flowers and the community outweighs Harry's, and Harry came with notice; a narrowly tailored injunction (shields, reduced hours, directional lighting) is plausible.

issues.name: Remedy – compensatory damages
issues.rule: Nuisance plaintiffs may recover compensatory damages for diminution in property value (permanent nuisance) or loss of use and enjoyment/annoyance and discomfort, plus mitigation costs (curtains, shutters); damages may be awarded in lieu of an injunction.
keyFacts: Harry bought an expensive new home
light enters his windows 24 hours a day
issues.analysis: Harry can recover for loss of use and enjoyment and cost of blackout measures or diminished value; knowledge of the light may reduce the amount since the price may reflect it.

issues.name: Remedy – punitive damages and other
issues.rule: Punitive damages require malice, oppression or fraud (conscious disregard); nominal damages and self-help abatement are other options.
keyFacts: Flowers posted warning signs
Flowers refused to turn off the light but acted for business reasons
issues.analysis: No malice: Flowers acted for a legitimate business purpose and warned neighbors, so punitive damages are unlikely.

notes: Student answers disagree on whether coming to the nuisance bars relief; the correct rule is that it is a factor only. Reviewer may want to check how much weight to give trespass-by-light.

issues.name: Steve – conspiracy to commit murder
issues.rule: Conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to commit an unlawful act with specific intent to achieve its objective; many jurisdictions (including California) require an overt act by a conspirator. Conspiracy does not merge with the completed target offense, and Wharton's Rule does not apply to murder because it does not inherently require two parties.
keyFacts: Will asked Steve to kill Adam and Steve accepted
Steve assaulted and killed Adam
issues.analysis: Agreement plus intent to kill is shown and the assault is an overt act; Steve is guilty of conspiracy in addition to murder.

issues.name: Steve – assault and battery (merger)
issues.rule: Assault is an attempted battery or intentional creation of reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact; battery is the intentional unlawful application of force. Lesser included offenses merge into the completed greater offense and cannot support separate convictions.
keyFacts: Steve assaulted Adam late at night on a dark, deserted street
Adam resisted vigorously
issues.analysis: Both are established but merge into murder (or at most are charged in the alternative).

issues.name: Steve – murder: malice and homicide
issues.rule: Murder is the unlawful killing of a human being with malice aforethought: intent to kill, intent to inflict serious bodily injury, reckless indifference to human life (depraved heart), or felony murder. Causation (actual and proximate) must be shown.
keyFacts: Steve is a professional assassin hired to kill Adam
Steve succeeded in killing Adam
Steve said he would kill Adam anyway
issues.analysis: Steve acted with intent to kill, so malice and causation are clear.

issues.name: Steve – first-degree murder (premeditation and deliberation)
issues.rule: First-degree murder is a willful, deliberate, premeditated killing (or murder by enumerated means or felony murder); California treats a plan to kill (including lying in wait) as premeditation.
keyFacts: Steve accepted the contract and planned to kill Adam
he was scheduled to kill Adam
assaulted him late at night on a deserted street
paid professional assassin; refused Will's cancellation
issues.analysis: Contract killing planned in advance is classic premeditation and deliberation; first-degree murder is the likely charge.

issues.name: Steve – felony murder / second-degree murder
issues.rule: Felony murder requires a killing during an independent inherently dangerous felony; assault/battery merges with the homicide and cannot be the predicate (merger doctrine). Second-degree murder is any malicious killing not first degree.
keyFacts: only assault/battery on Adam is described
issues.analysis: Felony murder is unavailable; second-degree murder is a fallback if premeditation were not proved.

issues.name: Steve – self-defense
issues.rule: Self-defense requires a reasonable belief of imminent unlawful force; an initial aggressor may not claim it unless he withdraws and communicates withdrawal or the victim escalates to deadly force beyond the aggressor's.
keyFacts: Adam resisted so vigorously as to put Steve's life at risk
Steve initiated the assault intending to kill
issues.analysis: Steve was the aggressor and never withdrew, so self-defense fails.

issues.name: Steve – manslaughter / mitigation
issues.rule: Voluntary manslaughter requires adequate provocation (heat of passion, no cooling off) or imperfect self-defense; involuntary manslaughter involves criminal negligence or misdemeanor-manslaughter and does not apply to intentional killings.
keyFacts: no provocation by Adam
Steve planned the killing
issues.analysis: No mitigating facts; Adam's resistance was a response to Steve's own attack, so manslaughter does not apply.

issues.name: Will – solicitation
issues.rule: Solicitation is asking, encouraging or inducing another to commit a felony with intent that it be committed; the crime is complete when the request is made, and later withdrawal is not a defense (though it may bear on mitigation). It merges into the completed target crime or conspiracy.
keyFacts: Will asked Steve to kill Adam
Will's motive: Adam was a business rival
issues.analysis: Solicitation was complete upon the request, regardless of the later change of mind.

issues.name: Will – conspiracy and Pinkerton liability
issues.rule: A conspirator is liable for the conspiracy itself and, under Pinkerton (and in some states only the target crime), for reasonably foreseeable crimes of co-conspirators in furtherance; here the murder is the very object of the conspiracy.
keyFacts: Steve accepted Will's request
Steve killed Adam
issues.analysis: Will conspired with Steve and the murder was the object of the conspiracy; conspiracy liability attaches and, absent withdrawal, murder liability under Pinkerton.

issues.name: Will – accomplice liability for murder
issues.rule: An accomplice is one who, with intent that the crime be committed, aids, abets, counsels or encourages the principal; he is liable for the target crime and natural and probable consequences.
keyFacts: Will hired and encouraged Steve to kill Adam
Steve killed Adam
issues.analysis: Will encouraged and procured the murder with intent, so he is an accomplice to first-degree murder unless he effectively withdrew.

issues.name: Will – withdrawal
issues.rule: Withdrawal from a conspiracy after the agreement does not erase conspiracy liability but cuts off liability for later crimes only if communicated to co-conspirators in time; for accomplice liability the accomplice must also neutralize his prior assistance or encouragement (e.g., warn the victim or police) or make a substantial effort to prevent the crime. Withdrawal is not a defense to solicitation or completed conspiracy.
keyFacts: Will told Steve he had changed his mind and no longer wanted Adam killed
Steve said he would kill Adam anyway
issues.analysis: Will's mere notice to Steve, with no effort to stop him or tell authorities, is ineffective since the plan was already set in motion; Will remains liable for conspiracy, solicitation and probably murder, though he has a sympathetic argument.

notes: Jurisdictions differ on Pinkerton and on withdrawal standard; California does not follow Pinkerton in the same way for non-target offenses but the murder here is the target. Wharton's Rule discussion in Answer A is inapplicable to murder.

issues.name: Abe v. Gary – assault
issues.rule: Assault is an intentional act creating in the plaintiff a reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact. Intent means purpose or substantial certainty; actual fear/awareness is required, and no physical contact is needed.
keyFacts: Gary yelled at Abe and threw a rock at him
Abe ducked, and the rock missed him
Abe is a 6-year-old
issues.analysis: Throwing a rock at a child who sees it coming and ducks satisfies intent, imminence and apprehension; Gary is liable for assault.

issues.name: Abe v. Gary – battery (not made out) / transferred intent
issues.rule: Battery requires harmful or offensive contact; an attempt that misses is not battery.
keyFacts: the rock missed him
issues.analysis: No contact occurred, so no battery; the claim is assault only.

issues.name: Defense of property
issues.rule: One may use reasonable, non-deadly force to prevent a tort against property after a request to desist where practicable; force likely to cause serious injury is not privileged merely to protect property, and force must be proportionate.
keyFacts: Gary is a groundskeeper who yelled 'get out of the flower beds!'
Abe is a 6-year-old running through flower beds
rock thrown at him
issues.analysis: Hurling a rock at a small child to protect flowers is excessive, so the privilege fails (deadly or dangerous force is never justified to protect property).

issues.name: Intentional infliction of emotional distress
issues.rule: IIED requires extreme and outrageous conduct, intent or recklessness, causation, and severe emotional distress.
keyFacts: Gary threw a rock at a 6-year-old child
issues.analysis: Conduct may be outrageous, but there are no facts showing severe distress, so the claim is weak.

issues.name: Remedies against Gary
issues.rule: Assault permits nominal and compensatory damages for emotional harm without proof of physical injury, and punitive damages for malicious conduct.
keyFacts: Abe was not hit
issues.analysis: Abe can recover at least nominal damages and possibly punitives for the malicious act.

issues.name: Betty v. Slideco – strict products liability: design defect
issues.rule: A commercial seller is strictly liable for physical injuries caused by a defective product that was defective when it left its control and used in a foreseeable manner. A design is defective under the consumer expectation test (California: also risk-benefit burden shifts to defendant) or if a reasonable alternative design would have avoided the risk.
keyFacts: metal slide manufactured and sold by Slideco
surface became very hot on typical summer days
reached 140 degrees
Betty sustained burns on her legs
issues.analysis: A slide that predictably reaches 140 degrees on ordinary summer days is unsafe beyond what a consumer expects; feasible alternatives (plastic, shading, other materials) exist, so a design defect is likely.

issues.name: Strict liability – failure to warn
issues.rule: A product is defective if the seller fails to give adequate warnings of non-obvious foreseeable dangers.
keyFacts: no mention of any warning on the slide
users are 6-year-old children
issues.analysis: A warning about burn risk would have been required and young children cannot read or heed signs, so a failure-to-warn claim is plausible but secondary to design defect.

issues.name: Strict liability – manufacturing defect, proper parties, and causation
issues.rule: Manufacturing defect exists when the product departs from its intended design; plaintiff must be a foreseeable user and defendant a commercial seller in the chain; actual and proximate causation required.
keyFacts: Slideco manufactured and sold
slide performed as designed on a typical day
issues.analysis: No manufacturing defect because the slide worked as designed; Slideco is a proper defendant, Betty a proper plaintiff, and the burns are directly caused by the heat.

issues.name: Negligence against Slideco
issues.rule: Manufacturer owes a duty of reasonable care in design and warnings to foreseeable users (no privity needed); breach is judged by risk-utility (Hand formula); then causation and damages.
keyFacts: Slideco knew or should have known its metal slide gets very hot
burns on her legs
issues.analysis: Reasonable manufacturer would have chosen a different material, shielding, or warnings; negligence is provable but requires proving fault, which strict liability does not.

issues.name: Breach of implied warranty of merchantability (UCC 2-314)
issues.rule: A merchant seller impliedly warrants goods are fit for their ordinary purpose; privity and notice issues are relaxed for personal injury to foreseeable users in many states (UCC 2-318).
keyFacts: Slideco is the manufacturer and seller
a slide is meant for children to slide on
issues.analysis: A slide that burns children in ordinary weather is not fit for its ordinary purpose; warranty claim viable, though Betty's lack of privity and notice are issues.

issues.name: Defenses – contributory/comparative negligence, assumption of risk, Jane's negligence
issues.rule: A child's conduct is judged by that of a child of like age, intelligence and experience; a 6-year-old using a slide as intended is not negligent and cannot appreciate the risk for assumption of risk; a babysitter's negligence is not imputed to the child.
keyFacts: Betty is 6 years old
climbed the ladder and went down the slide normally
Jane was the babysitter
issues.analysis: Defenses fail: Betty acted as a child would and neither she nor Jane's supervision will reduce recovery; common industry use of metal is not a defense.

issues.name: Carl v. Jane – duty (special relationship / voluntary assumption)
issues.rule: There is generally no duty to protect another, but a duty arises from a special relationship or voluntary assumption of care; a babysitter in charge of a child must supervise with reasonable care.
keyFacts: Jane, a babysitter, took three 6-year-olds to the playground
Carl is 6 years old
issues.analysis: Jane assumed custody and supervision of Carl, so she owed a duty of reasonable supervision.

issues.name: Carl v. Jane – breach
issues.rule: Breach is failure to act as a reasonable person (here, a reasonable babysitter) would; consider foreseeability of harm and burden of precautions (Hand formula).
keyFacts: Jane was too occupied texting on her cell phone
Carl kicked the ball into the street and ran to retrieve it
issues.analysis: Texting while watching three young children near a street is below the standard of care; breach likely.

issues.name: Carl v. Jane – causation and superseding cause (speeding motorist)
issues.rule: Plaintiff must show actual cause (but-for) and proximate cause (foreseeable harm). A third party's negligence is a superseding cause only if unforeseeable; a foreseeable intervening negligent act does not cut off liability, and defendants are jointly and severally liable for economic damages (several only for non-economic under California Prop 51).
keyFacts: motorist was driving 40 mph in a 25 mph zone
Carl was struck and injured
issues.analysis: Running into the street and being hit by a car is the very risk that supervision guards against, so the driver's speeding is a foreseeable concurrent cause and Jane stays liable (with apportionment).

issues.name: Carl v. Jane – defenses and damages
issues.rule: A 6-year-old is held to a child standard of care; comparative fault may reduce recovery. Assumption of risk requires subjective appreciation of the risk. Damages include medical expenses, pain and suffering.
keyFacts: Carl is 6 and was chasing a ball
Carl was injured when struck by the car
issues.analysis: Carl's chasing the ball is ordinary child behavior, so little or no reduction; Jane may seek apportionment against the motorist.

notes: Question includes a negligent-supervision claim only against Jane; the motorist is not a call-of-the-question party but relevant to causation and apportionment.

issues.name: UCC Article 2 applies; merchants
issues.rule: UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods; a merchant deals in goods of the kind or holds himself out as having specialized knowledge, triggering special merchant rules (firm offers, confirmatory memos, 2-207).
keyFacts: 100,000 widgets
Manufacturer makes widgets; Wholesaler resells them to retailers
issues.analysis: Widgets are goods and both parties are merchants, so UCC merchant rules apply.

issues.name: Formation of the oral contract
issues.rule: Under UCC 2-204 a contract may be made in any manner showing agreement; an offer is accepted by any reasonable expression of assent, and open terms may be filled by gap-fillers as long as quantity is stated.
keyFacts: Wholesaler ordered 100,000 widgets at $5 each for delivery February 8
Manufacturer said 'It's a deal'
issues.analysis: The phone call produced a binding oral contract at $5 per widget, delivery Feb 8, subject to Statute of Frauds.

issues.name: Statute of Frauds – merchant's confirmatory memo (UCC 2-201(2))
issues.rule: Goods contracts of $500 or more must be in a writing signed by the party to be charged stating quantity. Between merchants, a written confirmation sufficient against the sender satisfies the statute against the recipient unless the recipient objects in writing within 10 days of receipt; it removes the SOF defense but not the need to prove the contract.
keyFacts: contract for $500,000
February 2 signed memorandum confirming the agreement and stating all terms
Manufacturer received and read it on February 3 and did not respond
issues.analysis: Wholesaler's signed memo states quantity and Manufacturer did not object in writing within 10 days (refusal came orally on Feb 8, within the period but not as a written objection), so SOF cannot be asserted against Manufacturer. The wrong price does not defeat sufficiency because only quantity is required.

issues.name: Memo's conflicting price term and parol evidence
issues.rule: A confirmatory memo that misstates the oral deal does not change the agreement; a memo signed by only one party that merely confirms is not an integration, and the oral agreement terms may be proved. Evidence of mistake or scrivener's error is admissible; the price remains $5.
keyFacts: Wholesaler misstated the price as $6 apiece
oral deal was at $5
issues.analysis: The price term is $5; Manufacturer did not assent to $6, and parol evidence rule does not bar proof of the oral agreement because the memo is not a final integrated writing of both parties.

issues.name: Additional arbitration term (UCC 2-207)
issues.rule: Between merchants, additional terms in a confirmation become part of the contract unless the offer limits assent, the term materially alters the contract, or the other party objects. A term that would surprise or hardship the other party (such as arbitration, which is rare in the industry) is material.
keyFacts: added term that any dispute is subject to binding arbitration
Manufacturer was surprised; term was rare in the industry
Manufacturer did not respond
issues.analysis: Arbitration clause materially alters the agreement and does not become part of the contract despite silence, so Wholesaler may sue in court (arbitration clause not binding).

issues.name: Breach by Manufacturer; no excuse (impracticability, unconscionability)
issues.rule: Failing to deliver when due is a breach. Impracticability (UCC 2-615) excuses only where an unforeseen contingency makes performance extremely burdensome; a market price increase alone is a foreseeable risk of a fixed-price contract. Unconscionability is judged at formation.
keyFacts: Manufacturer discovered on February 8 that the market price had climbed to $25
Manufacturer refused to deliver
issues.analysis: Manufacturer breached by refusing delivery on Feb 8; rising price does not excuse performance. Wholesaler is likely to prevail.

issues.name: Wholesaler's performance/tender and mitigation (cover)
issues.rule: Buyer must be ready to perform to recover; the buyer may cover under 2-712 and recover the difference, but failure to cover doesn't bar recovery of market-contract damages, and duty to mitigate does not require an unreasonable act.
keyFacts: substitute widgets available for $25 apiece
Wholesaler did not have the cash or credit to buy them
issues.analysis: Wholesaler could not cover, so recovery is measured by market-contract differential, not cover; inability to cover does not defeat the claim.

issues.name: Remedy – market price damages (UCC 2-713)
issues.rule: If the buyer does not cover, damages are market price at the time buyer learns of breach minus contract price, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved.
keyFacts: contract price $5
market price $25
100,000 widgets
issues.analysis: $20 x 100,000 = $2,000,000, plus incidental damages.

issues.name: Remedy – consequential damages (lost resale profits) (UCC 2-715(2))
issues.rule: Consequential damages include losses from general or particular requirements of which the seller had reason to know that could not reasonably be prevented by cover (foreseeable, certain, unavoidable); no double recovery.
keyFacts: Manufacturer knew Wholesaler was buying to resell
Wholesaler immediately contracted to resell at $15 apiece
issues.analysis: Manufacturer knew of resale in general but not the $15 price, and Wholesaler cannot recover both lost profit ($10/widget) and market differential ($20) for the same widgets; at most liability to sub-buyers may be added. Court likely awards the market differential.

issues.name: Remedy – specific performance (UCC 2-716)
issues.rule: Specific performance is available where goods are unique or in other proper circumstances, e.g., where the buyer is unable to cover.
keyFacts: substitute widgets available at $25
Wholesaler lacks cash or credit to cover
issues.analysis: Widgets are generic, but inability to cover can be 'other proper circumstances'; this is a close call, and damages are likely adequate in any event.

notes: Close calls: whether Manufacturer's Feb 8 refusal counts as a written objection within 10 days; whether lost-profit damages overlap with market differential.
